body_html:
A technical SEO audit checklist is a step-by-step review of whether search engines can crawl, render, and index your site, and whether pages load fast enough for real visitors. Work through crawlability, indexing, duplicate URLs, site speed, mobile rendering, and structured data, then fix whatever blocks the pages that matter most.

What a technical SEO audit covers

Technical SEO is the plumbing under your content. An audit answers three plain questions: can Google find your pages, can it understand and store them, and do they work well for people once they load. Great content and strong links can't help a page Google never reaches.

You don't need a big software budget to start. Google Search Console is free and shows what Google sees. A crawler such as Screaming Frog, or the site audit tools in Semrush or Ahrefs, shows what a bot finds when it follows your links. Comparing the two views is where most problems show up.

Before you start: set up your tools

  • Verify your site in Google Search Console. A domain property covers every version of the site (http, https, www, and subdomains) in one place.
  • List your most important URLs: the pages that bring in leads, sales, or calls. These get checked first and fixed first.
  • Run a full crawl of the site. If your pages rely on JavaScript to show content, turn on JavaScript rendering in your crawler.
  • Note who can change what: templates, server settings, redirects, and robots.txt often sit with different people.

Technical SEO audit checklist, part 1: crawlability

Crawlability means a search engine's bot can reach a page by following links and isn't told to stay away.

  1. Check robots.txt. Open yoursite.com/robots.txt and make sure it isn't blocking important folders, or the CSS and JavaScript files pages need to display. Remember that robots.txt controls crawling, not indexing. Google's introduction to robots.txt says it is not a mechanism for keeping a page out of Google; use a noindex tag or password protection for that.
  2. Find broken internal links. Your crawler's 4xx report lists links pointing to pages that no longer exist. Update the link at the source instead of leaning on redirects forever.
  3. Clean up redirects. Look for chains (page A redirects to B, which redirects to C) and loops. Point internal links straight at the final URL and use 301 redirects for permanent moves.
  4. Look for orphan pages. These are pages no other page links to. Compare your crawl against your XML sitemap and your top landing pages in GA4 to spot them.
  5. Check click depth. Important pages should be reachable within a few clicks of the homepage. Pages buried deep in the site tend to be crawled less often.
  6. Watch for server errors. 5xx errors in your crawl, or in the Crawl Stats report under Settings in Search Console, mean your server is turning bots away.

Part 2: indexing

Indexing is Google storing a page so it can appear in search results. Open the Page indexing report in Search Console. Google says not to expect every URL on your site to be indexed, since some are duplicates or have little useful content, so focus on whether your key pages are.

  1. Review why pages aren't indexed. Sort the reasons by count. "Crawled - currently not indexed" or "Discovered - currently not indexed" on pages you care about often points to thin or duplicate content, or weak internal linking.
  2. Hunt for stray noindex tags. These often slip in during a redesign or when a "hide from search engines" setting is left on after launch.
  3. Fix soft 404s. A soft 404 is a page that says "not found" but returns a success code. Return a real 404 or 410 status for pages that are truly gone.
  4. Inspect key URLs. The URL Inspection tool shows whether a page is indexed, which canonical Google chose, and a screenshot of how Google rendered it.
  5. Audit your XML sitemap. It should list only canonical, indexable pages that return a 200 status. Google's sitemap guidelines cap each file at 50,000 URLs or 50MB uncompressed, say Google ignores the priority and changefreq fields, and say lastmod is used only when it's consistently accurate.

Part 3: duplicate URLs and canonical tags

The same content often lives at several addresses: http and https, www and non-www, with and without a trailing slash, or with tracking parameters added. A canonical is the version you want Google to treat as the main one.

  • Pick one preferred version of your domain and 301 redirect the others to it.
  • Give each indexable page a self-referencing canonical tag with an absolute URL.
  • Make sure canonicals point to live, indexable pages, not to redirects or noindexed pages.
  • Check that your sitemap, canonical tags, and internal links all name the same URL.

Google's canonicalization guide treats redirects and rel="canonical" as strong signals and sitemap inclusion as a weaker one. It also warns against using robots.txt or noindex to choose a canonical.

Part 4: site speed and Core Web Vitals

Core Web Vitals are Google's three measures of real-world page experience: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP, loading), Interaction to Next Paint (INP, responsiveness), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS, visual stability). According to web.dev, a page passes when LCP is 2.5 seconds or less, INP is 200 milliseconds or less, and CLS is 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of visits.

  1. Start with the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console. It uses data from real Chrome users and groups similar URLs together, so one template fix can clear many pages.
  2. Run PageSpeed Insights or Lighthouse on each main template (home, service, product, blog) to see what's slowing it down.
  3. Common fixes: compress and correctly size images, set width and height on images and embeds to stop layout shifts, defer JavaScript that isn't needed right away, and trim third-party scripts you no longer use.

For a deeper walkthrough, see my guide on improving site speed and Core Web Vitals.

Part 5: mobile, rendering, and HTTPS

  • Google crawls and indexes the mobile version of your site, so confirm the mobile pages carry the same main content, headings, and links as desktop.
  • If content loads with JavaScript, check the rendered HTML in URL Inspection to confirm Google sees it.
  • Serve every page over HTTPS, redirect http to https, and fix mixed content (images or scripts still loading over http).

Part 6: structured data

Structured data is code that labels what a page is about, such as a business, product, article, or FAQ, using the Schema.org vocabulary. Test key pages with Google's Rich Results Test, fix errors, and make sure the markup matches what's visible on the page.

How to prioritize what you find

An audit can surface hundreds of issues. Sort them so the work goes where it counts:

  1. Anything stopping important pages from being crawled or indexed.
  2. Site-wide template problems, since one fix repairs many pages.
  3. Speed and Core Web Vitals on your highest-traffic templates.
  4. Cleanup items, like old redirects and minor duplicate titles.

Track each issue in a spreadsheet with the affected URLs, the fix, who owns it, and the date it was fixed. Re-crawl after each round to confirm the fix held.

How often should you run a technical SEO audit?

A full audit once or twice a year works for most small and mid-size sites, with a lighter monthly check of Search Console for new indexing errors, Core Web Vitals changes, and crawl problems. Always run one before and after a redesign, platform move, or domain change, since those are the moments when redirects break, noindex tags get left behind, and pages quietly drop out of the index.

Can you do a technical SEO audit yourself?

Yes, for the basics. Search Console, PageSpeed Insights, and a crawler will surface most crawl, indexing, and speed issues on a small site, and this checklist gives you the order to work in. Where it gets harder is diagnosing why a problem happens and fixing it safely, especially redirects, JavaScript rendering, and server settings. That's usually the point where a developer or SEO specialist saves time.

What's the difference between a technical SEO audit and a full SEO audit?

A technical SEO audit looks at the site's infrastructure: crawling, indexing, speed, mobile, security, and structured data. A full SEO audit adds content quality, keyword targeting, on-page optimization, backlinks, and competitors. Many people start with the technical side because content and link work only pays off once search engines can reach and index the pages you're improving.
